name: Shipibo-Conibo icaros healing songs
lineage: Shipibo-Conibo icaros healing-song tradition of the Ucayali river basin of the Peruvian Amazon, with cognate forms across the broader Western Amazonian shamanic-tradition area (Asháninka, Shuar, Yagua, and Cocama-Cocamilla parallel forms). Icaros are sung-spells learned by shamans (onaya in the Shipibo language) through master-apprentice transmission and through dieta-restricted-diet plant-spirit communications, then deployed during nocturnal ayahuasca-ceremony healing sessions in the maloca palm-thatch ceremonial hut. Each icaro is associated with a specific plant-spirit (the icaro of ayahuasca, the icaro of chacruna, the icaro of toé, the icaro of bobinsana, and so on), a specific therapeutic function (cleansing icaros, protective icaros, vision-amplifying icaros, calling-the-spirits icaros, mareación-managing icaros), and a specific named master-shaman lineage. Performance occurs in near-darkness with the shaman singing close to the individual patient, the icaro lasting from a few minutes to over an hour depending on therapeutic context. Vocal style features narrow-range melodic vocabulary, characteristic glissando-and-descending-cadence ornaments, the use of phlegmatic-rasp voice quality for certain icaros, and the optional accompaniment of shacapa leaf-bundle rattle (the canonical Amazonian shamanic-rhythm instrument). Bernd Brabec de Mori's 2015 monograph Die Lieder der Richtigen Menschen (Helbling) and the Phonogrammarchiv of the Austrian Academy of Sciences Shipibo collection constitute the principal scholarly documentation; the 2008 Peruvian INC Resolución 836 declared traditional ayahuasca practice as cultural-heritage at the national level. Distinguished from Mestizo-Peruvian ayahuasquero icaros by the Shipibo-Conibo language repertoire and indigenous-community ceremonial-functional context; distinguished from Yawanawa and Huni Kuin healing songs by Shipibo-specific dieta-and-plant-spirit lineage.
